title: Cyperus compactus: How to Spot and Control This Sedge in Rice
metaTitle: Cyperus compactus in Rice: Sedge ID and Control Guide
metaDescription: Cyperus compactus is a tall perennial sedge in lowland rice. See how to spot its round reddish brown heads and dig it out before it spreads.
excerpt: Cyperus compactus is a tall sedge weed of irrigated and rainfed lowland rice fields in the Philippines. It can live for more than one season, and it spreads by seed and by underground stems. This page shows how to spot it among your palay, how it hurts the crop, and how to control it before it spreads.

heroImage.alt: Cyperus compactus, a sedge weed of Philippine rice fields

blocks.text:
This damo is a sedge from the Cyperaceae family. It has no common English name, and PhilRice's weed list gives no Filipino local name for it either. So this page calls it by its scientific name, Cyperus compactus. You will find it in both irrigated and rainfed lowland rice fields.

It is usually a perennial, but some plants live for one season only. It spreads in two ways. First, it drops seeds that sprout when farmers prepare the field. Second, it sends out rhizomes, which are stems that creep under the soil and push up new shoots. Because these rhizomes stay hidden, a clump you cut at the surface can grow back from below. That is why digging works better than cutting with this sedge.

blocks.caption: Quick facts about Cyperus compactus
rows: Irrigated and rainfed lowland rice fields

blocks.text: Like other sedges, it has a solid stem with three sides and no nodes. Roll the stem between your fingers and you will feel its edges. The stems stand erect and can grow up to 70 cm tall. Its leaves feel spongy and grow about as long as the stem. At the top, look for a cluster of many big, round spikes made up of reddish brown spikelets.

items: Erect stems that can reach 70 cm, standing tall among young rice plants.
Soft, spongy leaves that give a little when you press them.
Leaves that reach about the same length as the stem itself.
A crowded top cluster of big, round spikes with reddish brown spikelets.
A solid, three sided stem with no joints, which marks it as a sedge, not a grass.

blocks.text:
Like most sedges, Cyperus compactus competes with palay for light, water and fertilizer. Its tall stems can shade young rice plants, while its roots draw on the same soil nutrients your crop needs. Because it can live past one season, an old clump keeps taking resources crop after crop.

When it flowers, its seeds can mix with harvested palay and lower the quality of the seed you keep. Thick clumps also give rats and insect pests a place to hide near the rice hills. If you leave it alone, its rhizomes slowly widen each patch.

items: Dig out each clump with a hoe or bolo and lift the rhizomes too, because pieces left in the soil can sprout again.
During land preparation, rake up rhizome pieces that come to the surface and dry them in the sun instead of leaving them in the mud.
Remove plants before the round heads turn reddish brown, so they cannot add seed to your field.
Clean bunds and canal edges near the paddy, since perennial clumps there can survive between crops and creep back in.

blocks.text: What to Do at Each Age of Your Rice

items: **0 to 5 days:** keep the soil saturated. Use a pre emergence herbicide only if the field had many weeds last season.
**6 to 10 days:** hand weed in transplanted rice. In direct seeded rice, this is the window for an early post emergence spray.
**11 to 20 days:** keep water in the field, weed by hand or with a rotary weeder, and let Azolla and the Altica beetle help. Spray only if those fail.
**21 to 30 days:** top up the water and keep weeding. Spray only if weeding fails.
**31 to 40 days (transplanted rice):** hand weed. A spray this late is only a rescue.
After any post emergence spray, bring the water back within 1 to 3 days at 3 to 5 cm and hold it for 4 to 5 days. Keep young rice above it.

blocks.text: Active Ingredients That Work on Sedges

If water and weeding cannot hold Cyperus compactus down, choose an active ingredient that works on sedges at the age of your rice. The table follows PhilRice recommendations. Shop by the ingredient on the label, never by the brand. If your field also has other kinds of weeds, the [weed control helper](/weeds#control) finds the ingredients that cover all of them.

blocks.text: Use only herbicides registered with the [Fertilizer and Pesticide Authority](/blog/fertilizer-and-pesticide-authority), and follow the label on the pack: the rate, the timing, the water and the protective clothing. Switch herbicide groups between seasons so the weeds do not learn to survive them. Our [guide to herbicides for rice](/weeds/herbicides-for-rice-weeds) explains the groups.
Keep Cyperus compactus Out Next Season

items: Plant clean, certified seed. Weed seeds mixed into the punla are the easiest way in.
Keep the seedbed, the canals and the bunds free of weeds, so seed does not wash or blow into the paddy.
Plow and harrow well, and rake out the runners, roots or pieces you turn up. A small piece left in wet soil can grow a new plant.
Pull escapes before their flower clusters turn brown, since one clump drops a great deal of tiny seed.
Keep the field clean after harvest and through the fallow, so fewer seeds build up in the soil for next season.

blocks.text: These steps work for every [sedge weed](/weeds/types-of-weeds) in the paddy, not only this one. The [weed management guide](/weeds/weed-management-in-rice) puts them in order for a whole season.

blocks.text: Questions Farmers Ask About Cyperus compactus

items.q: What is the common name of Cyperus compactus?
items.a: It has no widely used English name, and PhilRice's weed list gives no Filipino local name for it. So most people know it by its scientific name. When you report it to a technician, use that name or show a photo of its tall stems and round, reddish brown flower heads.

items.q: How do I control it in my rice field?
items.a: Prevention comes first. Use clean seed, level the field well and keep a steady water level. Next, dig out clumps by hand along with their rhizomes. If you need a herbicide, pick one made for sedges that fits the age of your rice, since perennial sedges can regrow from below. Always follow the FPA registered label.

items.q: Why does it grow back after I cut it?
items.a: It grows back because it is usually a perennial with rhizomes under the soil. Cutting only removes the top, while the rhizomes stay alive and push up fresh shoots. To stop it, dig out the whole clump, lift the rhizomes, and carry them out of the field to dry in the sun.
